newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: MILITARY TRAINING OPTION FOR YOUNG JOBLESS
The Prime Minister says the Government is keen to look at any proposal which will help reduce youth unemployment, including military training.
Speaking on Sydney Radio 2UE, John Howard, says a plan to allow young jobless people to do basic military training is just one option being considered as part of the work-for-the-dole-scheme.
Under the plan, the young unemployed can opt to undertake such training as a way of boosting their motivational skills.
Mr Howard says the proposal isn't a central part of the scheme and hasn't yet gone before Cabinet.
HOWARD SAYS SOME DEBATE OVER EXPENSES "PETTY"
Prime Minister John Howard says the recent debate over the issue of Parliamentary entitlements is not likely to be resovled.
This follows renewed public criticism of MPs' salaries and expense allowances in the wake of rorting allegations against Independent Senator Mal Colston.

The Government is moving to clamp down on potential mis-use of entitlements but Mr Howard's told Sydney Radio 2-UE the issue's become petty, for example, strutiny of the use of Parliamentary letterheads.
Mr Howard says there's a tendency to dwell on such things, even though it's unlikely there'll ever be a situation where all people are satisfied.
FEARS CYLCONE JUSTIN IS INTENSIFYING
The weather bureau says Tropical Cyclone Justin appears to be intensifying, while remaining stationary off the Queensland coast.
North Queensland communities are on alert as gale force winds and rains, produced by the huge pressure system, lash the coast.
It's feared tidal surges will inundate homes, and small vessel owners have been urged to seek safe harbour.
The category two cyclone has already caused dramatic rescues, affected a massive US-Australian military exercise in Central Queensland, and forced coal ports to turn ships away.
Justin's expected to move slowly towards the north Queensland coast during the day or so.
CONCERN OVER BRYANT BOOK

Concerns have been raised about plans by a former lawyer of Port Arthur killer Martin Bryant to write a book about the case. Lawyer John Avery will try to meet with his former client this week to ask whether he can go ahead with the book.
Mr Avery says he has tapes of more than a dozen interviews with the mass murder, as well as drawings by Bryant of his impressions of the Port Arthur massacre.
Bryant's affairs are now handled by a trustee, and there's concern about whether the disclosure of solicitor-client dealings is in the client's interests.
The issue may be raised at a meeting today of Tasmania's Law Society's executive committee.
CONCERNS OVER RE-OPENING OF NSW TEACHER CASES

The New South Wales Education Minister, John Aquilina, has defended the government's actions in re-opening the cases of teachers with sexual misconduct allegations against them, which were not proven.
The NSW Council of Civil Liberties and a number of lawyers have criticised the re-examination of cases where a teacher has been aquitted of offences and returned to the classroom.
But Mr Aquilina there may be some cases where there could be ongoing concern about that teacher.
He says what needs to be assessed is whether or not having a person in charge of children in a school or classroom warrants an unexceptable risk as far as those students are concerned.
The Minister says different measures and standards need to be used in relation to that sort of environment, rather than used in a court or to determine if charges are laid.
STRIKE COSTS GRAND PRIX "MILLIONS"
A drop in attendance of more than 100-thousand spectators at the Melbourne Grand Prix is being blamed on the weekend transport workers strike.

Race organiser, Judith Griggs says the industrial turmoil has damaged the Grand Prix's image overseas and cost millions of dollars. Ms Griggs says only 239 thousand people attended the four-day event..a drop of 112-thousand from last year.
She says it doesn't do Australia's international standing any good if major events can be effectively held to ransom by third party disputes.
DEVASTATING IMPACT OF UNION CLAIM PREDICTED
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry says if granted, the impact of the ACTU's "living wage" claim would be immediate and devastating.
The Chamber says unemployment numbers would race past one-million, inflation and interest rates would rise, and investment growth would come to an immediate halt.
Unions are seeking an increase of eight and three-quarters per cent on all award rates of pay, estimated to cover 47 per cent of award workers.
The Industrial Relations Commission is due to hand down its decision on the claim sometime this month.
Instead of an across-the-board increase in award wages, the Chamber wants the decision to provide further momentum towards enterprise negotiations.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
